issues.legal_issue: A petition alleging that public action procedurally violates a fundamental right is maintainable under the constitutional remedy jurisdiction.
material_facts: The petitioners challenged the proposed and completed removal of their dwellings as violating fundamental rights.
They argued that the procedure used to remove the dwellings was arbitrary and unfair.
issues.conclusion: The petitions were maintainable under Article 32 because an aggrieved person may invoke that jurisdiction where action against them is procedurally ultra vires.
issues.legal_principle: Under Article 32, a person may seek enforcement of fundamental rights where public action is procedurally ultra vires. The Court followed Naresh Shridhar Mirajkar v. State of Maharashtra and referred to Smt. Ujjam Bai v. State of Uttar Pradesh.

predicates.fundamental_rights_enforcement_petition: A person brings a proceeding seeking enforcement of a fundamental right.
predicates.public_action_challenged_as_procedurally: The person alleges that public authorities acted through a procedure that unlawfully infringed the right.

issues.definition: When a person seeks enforcement of a fundamental right against public action alleged to be procedurally unlawful, the constitutional remedy jurisdiction is available.

issues.legal_issue: A person cannot be estopped from asserting or enforcing a fundamental right by a concession or undertaking in an earlier proceeding.
material_facts: In an earlier proceeding, the petitioners had conceded that they had no fundamental right to construct dwellings on public ways and had undertaken not to obstruct their demolition after an agreed date.
They later asserted that removing their dwellings would violate their fundamental rights, including the right to life.
issues.conclusion: The earlier concession and undertaking did not prevent the petitioners from asserting their fundamental rights in the later proceeding.
issues.legal_principle: There can be no estoppel against the Constitution, and an individual cannot barter away or waive fundamental rights. The Court relied on Basheshar Nath v. The Commissioner of Income Tax, Delhi, and discussed the connection between estoppel and waiver.

predicates.fundamental_rights_challenge: A person challenges public action as violating a fundamental right.
predicates.earlier_concession_or_undertaking_about_: In an earlier proceeding, the person conceded or undertook that they would not assert the fundamental right at issue.

issues.definition: A person who challenges public action as violating a fundamental right may still assert that right despite an earlier concession or undertaking not to do so.

issues.legal_issue: The right to life includes the right to livelihood where deprivation of livelihood would deprive a person of the means to live.
material_facts: The petitioners lived in pavement or slum dwellings near their work because their modest means made other housing and commuting impracticable.
The evidence and circumstances showed that eviction would cause many people in their position to lose their jobs and means of livelihood.
Their occupations were not alleged to be illegal or immoral.
issues.conclusion: The right to life under Article 21 includes the right to livelihood, and deprivation of livelihood must be according to just, fair and reasonable procedure established by law.
issues.legal_principle: The Court interpreted Article 21 in light of Articles 37, 39(a) and 41. It relied on Munn v. Illinois and Kharak Singh v. State of Uttar Pradesh, and distinguished In Re: Sant Ram because the petitioners did not claim livelihood through an illegal or immoral occupation.

predicates.constitutional_right_to_life_claim: A person claims that public action threatens the constitutional right to life.
predicates.livelihood_is_a_means_of_survival: The person's work or livelihood provides the means necessary to live.
predicates.threatened_deprivation_would_remove_that: The threatened action would deprive the person of that means of livelihood.

issues.definition: When challenged public action would deprive a person of the livelihood necessary to live, a claim to the right to life includes protection of that livelihood.

issues.legal_issue: The right to reside and settle does not confer a right to occupy public ways for a private dwelling without authorization, and removal powers over such encroachments are constitutionally valid when reasonably exercised.
material_facts: The dwellings occupied pavements, footpaths, roads or other public property intended for public passage or another public purpose.
The occupants had no authorization to use that public property for dwellings.
The occupation obstructed public passage and interfered with public safety and municipal functions.
issues.conclusion: No person has a right to encroach on public ways or other property reserved for public purposes. The relevant municipal removal provisions were not unreasonable in the circumstances and were constitutionally valid.
issues.legal_principle: Articles 19(1)(e) and 19(1)(g) do not authorize private occupation of public property. Sections 312, 313 and 314 of the Bombay Municipal Corporation Act, read with section 3(w), provide for removal of obstructions and encroachments; sections 61 and 63 describe relevant municipal duties and powers. The Court relied on Hickman v. Maisey in explaining the distinction between legitimate passage and unauthorized use of a public way.

predicates.constitutional_challenge_to_removal: A person challenges the constitutionality of public authorities' action to remove an occupation from public property.
predicates.public_property_is_reserved_for_passage_: The occupied property is set aside for public passage or another public purpose.
predicates.private_dwelling_is_unauthorized: A person uses the public property as a dwelling without authorization.

issues.definition: When an unauthorized private dwelling occupies property reserved for public passage or another public purpose, there is no right to remain there and the removal authority is valid.

issues.legal_issue: A statutory discretion to remove an encroachment without notice must be exercised reasonably, with a hearing as the ordinary rule and without a hearing only where circumstances justify that departure.
material_facts: The municipal provision authorized the Commissioner to remove encroachments without notice but did not command removal without notice in every case.
The Commissioner removed dwellings without giving prior notice or an opportunity to be heard.
The petitioners could have raised matters such as whether an encroachment existed, whether it caused public inconvenience, or whether time to leave was warranted.
issues.conclusion: The provision was to be read as giving discretion to remove with or without notice. That discretion had to be exercised reasonably; a hearing was the ordinary rule, and dispensing with it was permissible only in circumstances warranting an exception, such as urgency.
issues.legal_principle: Article 21 requires fair, just and reasonable procedure. Natural justice ordinarily requires an opportunity to be heard, and an exception must be justified by circumstances such as urgency. The Court relied on Maneka Gandhi v. Union of India, E.P. Royappa v. State of Tamil Nadu, Francis Coralie Mullin v. Administrator, Union Territory of Delhi, and S.L. Kapoor v. Jagmohan, among other cases. It construed section 314 of the Bombay Municipal Corporation Act as discretionary rather than as a general command to act without notice.

predicates.public_action_proposes_to_remove_an_encr: A public authority proposes to remove a person's occupation as an encroachment.
predicates.affected_person_can_raise_relevant_objec: The affected person could raise a relevant objection or request concerning the proposed action.
predicates.circumstances_make_prior_hearing_impract: The circumstances make a prior opportunity to be heard impracticable, for example because urgency requires immediate action.

issues.definition: A person affected by a proposed removal must have a reasonable opportunity to be heard when relevant objections can be raised and the circumstances do not make a prior hearing impracticable.

issues.legal_issue: Resettlement assurances and protections for identified and established settlements must be implemented, and eviction must be delayed to reduce hardship.
material_facts: The government had decided to provide alternate pitches to pavement dwellers identified in or recorded during a census and alternate accommodation to identified slum dwellers.

The government had a policy of not normally demolishing long-established, improved settlements unless the land was required for a public purpose, in which case alternative sites or accommodation would be provided.
The Court found that eviction disrupted the economic life of affected households and directed that settlements not be removed until one month after the current monsoon season.
issues.conclusion: The government had to provide alternate pitches to pavement dwellers recorded in the census and alternate accommodation to slum dwellers who were censused and given identity cards. Long-established, improved slums were not to be removed unless the land was required for a public purpose, in which case alternatives had to be provided. The government was directed to pursue its housing and upgrading programmes, and removal was deferred until one month after the end of the current monsoon season.
issues.legal_principle: The Court required the government to honour assurances made in the proceedings and applied the stated resettlement policies to identified and long-established settlements. It also relied on the need to minimize hardship from eviction and on the State's responsibilities reflected in the Directive Principles, including Articles 39(a) and 41.

predicates.eviction_or_resettlement_proceeding: Public authorities are proceeding with eviction or resettlement of residents from a settlement.
predicates.affected_residents_are_census_identified: The affected residents were identified through a census or live in a settlement that has existed for a long time and has been improved.

issues.definition: In an eviction or resettlement proceeding involving census-identified residents or a long-established, improved settlement, the government's resettlement assurances and protections to reduce hardship must be implemented.
